newsitem.title: TURKEY: Angry Turkish protests turn on ruling Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Angry Turkish protests turn on ruling Islamists.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists are on the defensive as a grassroots protest against state corruption, now in its fourth week, has increasingly turned its fire on the government's anti-secular policies.
Launched on February 1 as a nightly, one-minute outpouring of outrage at alleged state ties to gangsters and death squads, the protests have taken on a distinctly anti-Islamist complexion.

That has raised the stakes for Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and his Islamist Welfare Party, which played on its clean image to win a slim plurality in general polls in December, 1995. His coalition now clings to a narrow majority.

In a scene reminiscent of bigger gatherings elsewhere in the Balkans, crowds in Istanbul's secularist strongholds on Saturday night blew whistles, clapped in unison and shouted anti-government and anti-Islamist slogans.
Simliar popular protests, a rarity in Turkey, have been held each evening in the capital Ankara and other cities and towns. Press reports suggest broad participation in many urban areas.
"If you stay silent, they'll come for you next," chanted hundreds of people off Istanbul's Taksim Square, a stronghold of Turkish secularism and the former Christian "capital" of the Ottoman empire.

Attempts by Welfare to stem the protests, in which Turks were asked to turn off their lights every evening at 9 p.m. for "one minute of darkness for eternal light", have backfired. And the government and its supporters are clearly worried.

"The protest has gone sour," declared a headline at the weekend in the moderate Islamist daily Zaman. "The one-minute darkness campaign to throw light on (the scandal) is increasingly turning away from its purpose."
The interior ministry last week ordered local forces around the country to be on alert in case of violence.

But there was no sign of any trouble in Istanbul, where passersby quickly joined in the rally, as apartment dwellers and nearby bars and cafes flicked their lights off and on. Within five minutes it was all over.

"We're doing this for freedom of thought, we don't want our country to be like Iran," said one student in the crowd, as police fidgeted with their batons and a plainclothes officer filmed the protesters.
"I don't want my mother or sister to have to go around with her head covered all the time," said the student, 22, who declined to give his name.
"This is against corruption, against Erbakan, against (Islamic) Sharia law," said another marcher.
Erbakan, who earlier denounced the protesters as "seditious" and "troublemakers", has inflamed public opinion and secularist armed forces with attempts to introduce Islam into public life.

Announced policies, most later withdrawn or toned down, included lifting a ban on Islamic headscarves in government offices, overland haj pilgrimages to the holy city of Mecca and construction of showpiece mosques in secularist districts.

In Ankara, about one third of households in the posh districts of Gaziosmanpasa and Cankaya turned off their lights for 60 seconds. One man played a trumpet from his balcony, while others beat pots and pans in the streets or touched off sirens.

Private television channels showed the darkened windows at a big military housing complex on the edge of the capital, a striking reminder of the armed forces' traditional role as defender of the officially secular system.
Earlier this month the army paraded tanks through an Islamist district, in a more muscular expression of displeasure.

And Turkey's big Alevi community, a heterodox Moslem sect, threw its weight behind the protests after Welfare's justice minister -- repeating a traditional slander -- implied sect members used the "minute of darkness" to practice incest.

The Alevi shantytowns that ring Ankara, as well as the sect's stronghold of Tunceli, in eastern Turkey, have erupted in noise each evening since Justice Minister Sevket Kazan's remarks. A bungled public apology only made things worse.
